World.title: Doha diary: A historian amid the Iran war
World.content:
(Renowned historian and author, Rila Mukherjee, was scheduled to fly from the USA to India by Qatar Airways [QA] on February 25, 2026. Her route—Shreveport–Dallas Fort Worth–Doha–Kolkata—was expected to bring her to Kolkata on the night of February 26 or in the early hours of February 27. However, as of March 8, she was still stranded in Doha. Qatar’s skies were closed due to the US-Israeli attack on Iran. QA’s commercial flights were suspended. At the time of writing, evacuation flights to India were scheduled to start soon. She reached home on 12 March.)

Today is 8 March. I am now camping out in Doha for the ninth day since 28 February. The Qatar airspace is shut and padlocked. The authorities have thrown away the key. Limited numbers of passengers are being flown to Europe and the Americas on evacuation flights (they are called ‘relief flights’) organised by QA, and relief flights to Africa and Asia will start from tomorrow. But for the time being, I am effectively marooned in Doha.

Doha is one of the largest airplane hubs in the world, and a cosmopolitan group of transit passengers has been put up by QA in the 4-star The Royal Riviera Hotel. The hotel is situated on Doha’s Corniche. It is an ageing hotel; not terribly posh, and the plumbing is a bit iffy. But it is well located, with comfortable rooms, and it is a clean and friendly hotel. I feel safe here. Its staff is composed of Asians (from Bangladesh, the Philippines, Sri Lanka, Nepal), North Africans (Algerians and Moroccans mostly) and some West Asians. All of them are helpful despite the pressures they are facing. They deal gracefully with the diverse demands and complaints of the passengers.

My room faces the Corniche and I can see the Persian Gulf from my window. As a maritime historian, this makes me very happy.

This country and its national airline are looking after us very well and, really, I have no complaints. QA’s representatives visit the hotel twice daily. There is no information forthcoming on my evacuation to Kolkata, and the greater part of passenger bags are still to arrive at the hotel. My South African neighbour says one of their bags has not been delivered; perhaps it is lost.

We are largely dependent on the clothes we have on our backs and those we had in our carry-on. Most of us are washing and drying them overnight. We have to use the hair dryer if they are still not dry.

My bags came in today, i.e., 8 March.

There are some elderly travellers. Many of them say that their medicines are running out. Mine will last another week.

Will I be able to get out by then?

We are told that a limited air corridor may open today; alternatively, we may be evacuated by the land route through Saudi Arabia to Riyadh (this would take around seven hours), where a leased QA aircraft may take us to India. But we have to make our own arrangements for the Saudi e-visa and overland travel. This seems a risky enterprise. And whether this potential leased aircraft would fly me direct to Kolkata is not known. There is no clarity to date.

***

But if I was scheduled to arrive in Kolkata on 27 February (and the war broke out a day later, on 28 February), how is it that I am still in Doha

Ah, thereby hangs a tale!

It is a cautionary tale on buying air tickets with multiple connections, and what ensues when the first connection does not take off as per schedule.

***

I had spent nine weeks in Shreveport with my son and daughter-in-law and was scheduled to leave on 25 February. Unfortunately, my flight from Shreveport to Dallas Fort Worth (DFW) by QA’s codeshare partner American Airlines (AA) did not take off. We were told that the incoming flight had nose gear problems and therefore could not land. Ultimately it made an emergency landing. Fire engines, firefighters, EMTs and ambulances were standing by. Luckily, there was no fireball and there were no casualties. The vice-chair of my daughter-in-law’s department was on that flight; I bumped into him in the terminal as he deplaned, and he said that the landing had been really scary.

There were no more AA flights to DFW that day. Roo and Stephanie came back to the airport and took me home. I spent a restless night. I hate flying at the best of times.

I was put on the same AA flight the next day, on 26 February, but when I reached DFW I was told that my connection flight to Doha was full. Apparently, the AA staff at Shreveport Regional Airport knew there were no seats on that flight; nevertheless they sent me on to DFW hoping I would ‘sort out’ the matter with AA’s customer care there. The only ‘sorting out’ that AA did at DFW was to put me on a later QA flight to Doha on the same day, that is, late evening on 26 February. It was a smaller aircraft (not the Airbus 350 on which I was ticketed), the flight was cramped and some of my co-passengers were not very well behaved. One lady kept on drinking; she skipped the meal service and was quite abusive. Another one, African American, told me that as an ‘American’ she was superior to Asians. Right, I thought, we all know how you as a Black person got there!!!

In all my years of travelling I have never encountered such blatant racism.

When we reached Doha very late on the night of 27 February (almost 24 hours later due to the time difference with DFW), I had missed that evening’s flight to Kolkata!

No problem, QA’s customer care said, we’ll talk with AA as it is their problem. This took a while, so I went off to buy myself a snack at Brioche Dorée in the airport’s food court.

By then it was early morning on 28 February.

Readers, note the date!

***

AA agreed to comp me a room for the remainder of the night at The Royal Riviera Hotel. I was granted a 48-hour emergency visa by Qatar Immigration and I was shifted to the hotel on 28 February at 2 AM. QA’s ground staff helped me throughout. The room was comfortable, the bed looked inviting, and I went to sleep, confident that my Kolkata flight would take off as scheduled at 18.45 hours on that day itself (that is, 28 February). At that point, I was going to reach only 24 hours behind my original schedule.

I informed Kolkata and asked my driver to collect me from the airport accordingly.

***

On 28 February, I was woken around 8 AM by a strange sound from my cell phone. It was a very loud, continuous screech. I don’t have international roaming and I wondered who was calling me and what was happening. I saw a ‘Security Alert’ on my screen but the text was in Arabic. I started hearing thuds and bangs. Another alert, still in Arabic, came in.

What was going on? I was mystified.

I was now getting alerts in English. It said the US and Israel had jointly attacked Iran. US bases and embassies and consulates across the Gulf were vulnerable. Qatar was in this critical area. Sirens were going off. I started watching Al Jazeera and Richard Engel on NBC.

This was Day 1.

Smoke rises following an explosion, after Israel and the US launched strikes on Iran, in Tehran, Iran, February 28, 2026. PHOTO: REUTERS

By Day 2, the Gulf was not just lying in a war zone; it had been converted into a theatre of war. Doha was undergoing regular drone strikes and missile attacks.

Day 3 was relatively quiet. Apparently, Qatar and Iran had a phone conversation, and Qatar urged Iran to stop the strikes. But our temporary visas were extended by Qatar. This was an indication that the phone call was not conclusive. This war was not going to end anytime soon.

The Qatar–Iran conversation does not seem to have yielded the desired result. There is no relief from Iranian attacks. These now form the backdrop to our daily life at The Royal Riviera. Drone attacks and missile strikes re-started from Day 4. None of them target the downtown area; they target only the US base and industrial areas in Qatar. Most of the drones and missiles are successfully intercepted; the few that are not cause localised fires. The attacks usually happen around breakfast and lunch, and sometimes they occur very late at night or in the early morning hours. This means we are always in a state of extreme alert. It is jarring on the nerves. We can neither eat properly nor rest. We are getting stressed out.

But I must also mention that the attacks and interceptions sound more like Diwali patakas than the very loud explosions that one expects.

*** Days 4 till 9 (that is, till date) have seen this regional war extending from land to sea: from the Hormuz Strait to the Indian Ocean. This is now becoming very serious. Critical choke points like this strait have become a curse. Ports across the Gulf are lying idle; almost no cargo is getting through. But we have had no alerts today. Does this mean that Iran will not strike Qatar for the time being? Is this a temporary reprieve? Will relief flights be able to take off? ***

Some bags arrived at the hotel on Day 5. Mine were not among them.

By Days 6 and 7 we have more or less settled into what is turning out to be our semi-permanent home. The hotel is no longer very ‘royal’; it has taken on the character of a London bedsit. Or a council housing estate in one of the UK’s inner cities! Children play noisy games in the corridors, an oddly comforting sound among the explosions, security alerts and sirens that go on regularly.

I see an enormous solidarity among the travellers, both on my floor and when we meet up at meal times. I have a very nice South African couple next door who check on me each morning, always asking how I am faring (‘please don’t hesitate to knock if you face any difficulties’). They have even offered to take me out to buy clothes (this was before my bags arrived). Elegant MENA (Middle East North Africa) people greet me each day at breakfast, a young Pakistani financial analyst from Toronto shares his insights with me at the breakfast table, and a British couple advise me to carry my passport with me at all times (especially when I leave my room in case of an attack and subsequent fire). They kindly offered to buy me my medicines, although they are at least a decade older than me. A young school teacher from Geneva shares my table at dinner. I have not seen her lately; perhaps she has already been repatriated on one of the relief flights to Europe which started operating from Day 7. The British couple and the South Africans are still here; the Pakistani man left for Toronto early this morning. He was given only two hours’ notice and he phoned my room to say goodbye at 1.15 AM this morning.

***

What does my daily schedule look like?

It is like what I imagine a day at boarding school would be. Because it is Ramadan, the hotel starts the breakfast buffet from 3 AM, lunch is from 12 noon, and dinner is over by 7.30. The food served (although mild in taste and quasi-institutional as regards the daily menu, which does not rotate much in terms of items), is nevertheless amazingly varied as regards the cuisine: Arabic, Turkish, Italian, Spanish and South Asian (the last is not good at all). A lot of lemon is used in the preparations, but practically no onions. This may be due to the fact that there was an onion shortage; onions came in from India only on Day 5. There are loads of different kinds of salads, some bland European cheeses and diverse types of hummus. In addition, there is feta cheese, stuffed vine leaves, green and black olives, veg and non-veg samosas and spring rolls, koftas, and baba ghanoush or baingan bharta. Good cappuccinos and lattes. Flaky croissants and brioches, pastries and amazing Arabian/Persian/Yemeni sweets. A decadent baked (and often caramelised) bread pudding called Umm Ali is served at dinner. Obviously, the Qatari supermarkets are still well-stocked with FMCG. The Indian-origin Lulu supermarket chain has flown in a whole lot of perishable and non-perishable food items.

Strangely, no fresh fruit!

***

Gas prices have shot up.

I have given up watching the death and destruction on TV, and watch Looney Tunes, Anthony Bourdain, Fawlty Towers and Mr Bean instead. Priyam Paul, my editor at The Daily Star, has sent me some e-books which help to pass the time.

When I am not reading, or watching sitcoms, cartoons and travel and food documentaries, I reflect on what brought us to this war. I see the Persian Gulf from my room; it is still a brilliant blue. But it is also desolate since the Hormuz Strait was closed off. I see no cargo ships or container vessels; there are no cruise ships or tankers. For a maritime historian like me, this is not the Persian Gulf I know. After all, it has been a crossroads since recorded history! My India in the Indian Ocean World (2022) documents this history of two thousand years at the very least. Now, mobility is severely constrained.

Persian Gulf. Photo: Collected

We are living now in a world of fragmented geopolitics, of accelerated climate degradation, and of critical demographic shifts. The world is undergoing these changes along with increasingly disaffected groups of peoples, perhaps terrorists, some of them. We are seeing the rise of AI which, to my mind, is linked, along with the toxicity of social media, with the increasing authoritarianism that we see worldwide. It horrifies me when I see a young nation declare it will bring ‘civilisation’ to Iran. It disregards the fact that Iran-as-Persia predates Arab culture and is one of the world’s oldest culture areas. Not just the glory of Shi’ite Safavid Persia (1501–1736), which political theorists and analysts invoke when describing this civilisational space and whose heritage modern Iran draws on: think of the period from c. 550 BCE to 651 CE (Muslim conquest and start of Islamisation by the Rashidun Caliphate), when four mighty Persian empires ruled a large portion of the then-known world: Achaemenid, Seleucid, Parthian and Sassanian. Persia challenged Egypt, Greece and Rome, and then it faced up to the Ottoman and Russian empires. This memory of resistance of 2500 years will not be easily erased.

However, the total disregard of international law and the collapse of the rules-based order will usher in a new regional order in West Asia. This will impact on the Gulf states. Once-biblical Lebanon is almost destroyed by a rampant Israel. Syria has closed its borders. As a rogue USA intimidates Persia and trains its eye on the Caucasus and Azerbaijan, it also destabilises Iraq. Iranian Kurds based in Iraq have been reactivated. How will this impact on the Turkish Kurds? Turkey, a NATO country, is already feeling threatened.

The relatively young post-WW1 statelets in the Gulf will lose out in the violent reshuffle in the greater region. The Dubai story was already over. And Oman had lost its sheen even earlier. Financial and service centres will shift eastward—to Singapore or perhaps to KL. As will global airline hubs. The Gulf states will see their importance in location, business and finance diminish. They will have to reconsider their dependence on the USA which has now become a double-edged sword. Iran will endure, but perhaps in a new form. But it will not be erased from the map of the world.

World.title: André Béteille: A sociologist Bangladesh should read
World.content:
My first encounter with the ideas of Professor André Béteille was in July 1966 in an introductory sociology course at the University of Dhaka (at that time in East Pakistan) through Professor Tom Bottomore’s book, Sociology: A Guide to Problems and Literature (1962). The emphasis on general theory of social stratification for an explanation of the Indian caste system found its empirical reflection, as Bottomore refers to, in the work of Béteille, especially in Caste, Class and Power: Changing Patterns of Stratification in a Tanjore Village (1965).

My second encounter with him was in the Fall of 1975 at Dalhousie University, Halifax where I was writing my Master’s thesis under Professor Bottomore, and he referred to read me Béteille’s “Closed and open social stratification” (1966). Reading Béteille after nine years under the Maple tree, I began to admire his empirical depth, comparative methodology, and theoretical clarity, which reshaped my understanding of social hierarchies in India.

In the Christmas of 1976, I had an occasion to share some of my understanding of Béteille’s work. At that time, I was at York University, Toronto where I was doing my PhD. Professor K. Ishwaran, one of our faculty members, who wrote Tradition and Economy in Village India (1966), invited me for Christmas dinner-- Turkey with cranberry sauce, cooked by his Dutch wife. There we talked about the contribution of both Béteille and his supervisor M. N. Srinivas towards understanding the impact of social change on Indian social stratification.

In order to realistically understand contemporary caste hierarchy, Béteille emphasised the “other factors such as class and power” that “have to be considered as independent variables” (1966). It appeared to me highly useful for comparative empirical research. It creates a distance from traditional essentialist and ideological perspective of inequality.

Borrowed from Max Weber, he focused on multidimensionality of stratification and examined how status, economic resources, and political control interact to shape multifarious social order. This was a tremendous contribution in the field of stratification studies. Though he focused on rural stratification, the model is also applicable to the study of urban social stratification.

It is puzzling that in Bangladesh universities, both sociology and anthropology disciplines overlooked and neglected the Weberian model of multidimensional stratification system: anthropology remained spell-bound under the dichotomous model of rural “ashraf-atraf”; and sociology was locked in the iron cage of simplistic Marxist model of “land ownership” under the name of peasant studies. In spite of teaching Weber’s “Class, Status, Party” (1922/1946) in the universities, there is a marked absence of the application of Weberian model in the study of rural and urban complex social hierarchy. Probably in Bangladesh, this shows the intellectual bankruptcy of these disciplines, which are suffering from morbidity.

In fact, in order to understand contemporary social change in Bangladesh, especially its regime of accumulation under crony capitalism, it is essential to understand the nexus between power and class. The determining power of traditional property ownership in the formation of classes and consequent class consciousness has diminished in Bangladesh.

The notion of political capitalism advanced by Max Weber is also useful in understanding Bangladesh social stratification, especially class formation. The party consciousness along with ruling party affiliation, may give legitimate or illegitimate access to economic resources, thereby determining class position in terms of life opportunities and life style. This in turn, heavily influence commodification of prestige and honour; and becomes marker of status.

André Beteille (1934 - 2026). Photo: Collected

The rural and urban dispossession, which is an integral part of neoliberal and crony capitalism’s regime of accumulation, is also the progenitor of emergent lumpen bourgeoisie, whose class position do not correspond with their demeaning status position. Again, the traditional status group in Bangladesh, as Béteille found in his Tanjore village study with respect to traditional caste, suffer from status dislocation, having less access to power and economic resources. The ontology of inequality and hierarchy can best be understood by the Weberian epistemology.

I think study of this process of social change, and its impact on inequality in Bangladesh, is vital towards understanding Bangladesh society. The internationally acclaimed Indian empirical model provided by Béteille can be one of the best guides to study the intersectionality of class, status and power in both urban and rural Bangladesh. It is unfortunate that social sciences in Bangladesh have neglected such a significant social dynamic that affects all our lives.

In March 1989, Professor Abhijit Dasgupta, a colleague of Professor Béteille, facilitated my direct meeting with him. Professor Dasgupta was kind enough to arrange a seminar talk by me in the sociology department of Delhi School of Economics. After the seminar, I paid a visit to Professor Béteille’s office room. He was very warm and hospitable to offer tea to me and my wife. He spoke in Bangla and affirmed his Bangali origin. I felt very comfortable to have a vibe of Bengal. I mentioned to him how I came to know of his work à la Bottomore and Ishwaran. I was so surprised to experience his stock of knowledge mediated by modesty and simplicity. The meeting with professor Béteille during the short-lived spring of Delhi was one of the most memorable events of my life. I wish his conceptual and methodological clarity inspire the young Bangladeshi sociologists to break the chain of ignorance, myopic framework, and the hegemony of intellectual infantilism.

A.I. Mahbub Uddin Ahmed is a professor in the Department of Sociology at the University of Dhaka.

World.title: In praise of Mymensingh’s Bangla folk ballads
World.content:
Folk-ballads are living archives that represent the imagination, values, ideas, and aesthetics of the people to whom they belong. Bangla literature has a rich repertoire of folk ballads. We are, however, quite oblivious of this treasure trove and, therefore, there is a dearth of research on these folk elements.

Czech Indologist Dusan Zbavitel's Bengali Folk-Ballads From Mymensingh And The Problem Of Their Authenticity can be called a wonderful exception in this regard. It is considered to be the first literary study of the beautiful folk-ballads from Mymensingh. The study was published by the University of Calcutta in 1963.

A brief background of the book may not be irrelevant here. In 1923, Rai Bahadur Dineshchandra Sen edited a volume of epic songs from the Mymensingh District of the then Eastern Bengal under the title Maimansimha-gitika. The ballads were mainly collected by Chandra Kumar De, a literary activist from the area. In the following years, Dineshchandra published three more volumes of balladic texts containing epic songs from different parts of Eastern Bengal. The beautiful ballads received enthusiastic response and admiration in India and abroad. However, for some scholars these ballads were too good, and they shared doubts about the ‍antiquity, authenticity and folk character of these lores. Dusan Zbavitel found this uncertainty "highly regrettable" and undertook a study to assign to the ballads their proper place—"one of the high points of Bengali literature". Dr Zbavitel tried to find out: "what is it that makes them so excellent?"

Zbavitel confined his analysis to the study of the ballads originating in Mymensingh—41 ballads containing more than 21,000 verses. He took an arduous effort of analysing each of these 41 ballads to prove their originality and, I must say, he achieved his goal with marked success.

One key argument put forward by Zbavitel in favour of the originality of the gitikas from Mymensingh is that these ballads are not collected by a single person and, still, there are similarities among the ballads: identical images, and similar artistic approach and common inventory of similes and metaphors. So these ballads couldn't be the creation of a modern poet as suggested by some detractors.

According to Zbavitel, the most significant aspect of these folk ballads is that they are devoid of any religious implications. They generally show harmonious co-existence of the Hindu and Muslim communities, without religious bias on either side. Zbavitel points out the fact that most of the Hindu ballads were collected from Muslim singers, which shows, according to him, that these folk poems were enjoyed and appreciated by both the communities with the same eagerness. The secular outlook of the folk ballads is diametrically opposite to the explicit religious connotation of the classical Bangla literary texts such as Mangal-kavyas and Vaisnava literature.

Zbavitel extensively discusses the ideological and artistic approach of the ballad writers, verse and rhyme technique, and use of similes and metaphors in chapter three and four of the book. The most dominant motif, according to Zbavitel, is love. Even the historical and heroic epics can be grouped into this category.

As to the literary techniques, the ballad writers, being true to the characteristics of folk epics, do not try to introduce innovations in their lyrical dictions. They are content with the poetic means offered by their predecessors. They want to tell an interesting and touching story in a simple garb, fresh with country scenes and feelings.

Zbavitel also discusses the manner of preservation of the folk ballads—preserved, in most cases, in torsos. Referring to two versions of the same ballad, Maishal Bandhu, he argues, "The 'original' ballads [were] sometimes rewritten by another folk poet, or other poets, quite freely, without any scruples; whole portions, as well as individual couplets and verses, were taken over, others were replaced by newly replaced passages, and the story itself was often changed." The reasons behind such changes, according to Zbavitel, might be an effort to offer listeners a 'better' story than the original one.

Due to this oral nature of preservation, it is always difficult to prove the originality of folk elements. If we undertake an effort to study the folklore of Bangladesh, Zbavitel's book will be an invaluable companion guide.

Rabindranath Tagore wrote to Dinesh Chandra Sen in appreciation of the book Maimansimha-gitika, "Classical Bengali literary texts such as Mangal-kavyas are ponds dug on by order and at the expense of the rich, but Maimansimha-gitika is a source of exuberance from the deepest level of the heart of rural Bengal, a clear stream of genuine pain. There has never been such a creation of self-forgetting rasa [aesthetic joy] in Bengali literature." [translation by the author]

While celebrating the Bengali new year this Pohela Boishakh, may we remember the melody and the essence of communal harmony embedded in Maimansimha-gitika.

Shamsuddoza Sajen is a journalist and researcher. He can be contacted at [email protected].

World.title: Fizz takes three in Mumbai rout
World.content:
Pace sensation Mustafizur Rahman recorded his best bowling figures of the Indian Premier League today when he finished with 3 for 16 in Sunrisers Hyderabad’s 85-run victory over Mumbai Indians at Vishakhapatnam.

The three-wicket haul took the left-armer to joint-second in the wicket-takers’ list with a total tally of 13 scalps from nine matches. He is one short of Mitchell McClenaghan, who has taken 14 wickets in 10 matches.

The 20-year-old currently has the best bowling average, 15.61, and best economy rate, 6.15, amongs bowlers who have played at least eight matches in the tournament.

The Sunrisers Hyderabad might have depended on Mustafizur a number of times in the ongoing Indian Premier League, but today was a collective effort. Ashish Nehra, Bhuvaneshwar Kumar and Barinder Sran had reduced the Mumbai Indians to 49 for 6 in nine overs before Mustafizur was given the ball.

The wily left-armer sent back Hardik Pandya with his first ball with a cutter which Pandya failed to adjust himself against. Pandya attempted a slice through point, but the ball curled away to the hands of the keeper, with the umpire judging that out even though the television replays were inconclusive.

Then in the very first ball of his second over again, Fizz bowled yet another slower delivery which moved away from the batsman, getting the edge of Tim Southee on the way to the keeper.

The man from Satkhira returned got the scalp of McClenaghan in the final delivery of his third over, getting the batsman to offer a loopy catch to midwicket.

Mustafizur did not get to bowl a fourth over as David Warner gave the other bowlers their chance to mop up the tail. And they did efficiently, bundling out the hosts for just 92 runs in 16.3 overs.

Earlier, brilliant performances from Hyderabad openers, Warner and Shikhar Dhawan helped the team post 177. Dhawan scored 82 off 57 while Warner smacked 48 off 33. Yuvraj Singh also had a good time with the bat, scoring 39 off 23.

World.title: See where climate change is hitting Victoria's infrastructure hardest
World.content:
At least $57 billion worth of infrastructure in Victoria is at risk from more frequent and severe bushfires, floods and extreme heat.

Melbourne's road and rail networks will incur the greatest costs in infrastructural damage from natural disasters, a new report reveals.

The report published by Infrastructure Victoria looked at $318 billion worth of state-owned or regulated public networks and assets. It warns that more than $57 billion worth of assets are currently at risk of damage and shows costs could blow out beyond $71 billion in the coming decades.

Recent shocks to global fuel markets have brought supply chains into focus. But the physical networks that we rely on every day to move supplies, power our homes and keep communities safe are under threat as well, as the frequency and severity of disasters increase with a warming climate.

According to its authors, the Warning Signs report is a first of its kind in Australia and shows how extreme weather events will impact infrastructure across Victoria in 2030. It also forecasts how this could look in a "worst case" scenario in 2070.

But the report stresses that the financial fallout from these hazards could be mitigated by an array of cost-effective actions and funding measures to safeguard infrastructure now.

Identifying risk

Natural disasters are not a new phenomenon but their growing frequency and severity challenge the environment and conditions these structures were built to withstand.

"Our research highlights which assets are most exposed, which climate risks matter most and where risks are concentrated across the state", says Jonathan Spear, Infrastructure Victoria CEO.

"It shows where the Victorian government should act now to reduce future damage, service disruption and millions in recovery costs."

Overall, the report identified roads, rail, energy infrastructure and health assets as the most vulnerable sectors. The climate hazards with the highest potential costs are bushfires, followed by floods and extreme heat.

The report shows cities and towns generally have a higher value of infrastructure at risk from climate hazards. Melbourne and its surrounding areas will add the biggest share of damage costs from natural disasters, followed by regional centres including Geelong, Mildura, Shepparton, Portland and Bendigo.

Cost of flooded roads

Roads are the most valuable infrastructural asset at risk, with up to $20 billion worth of assets at risk in 2030.

Flood waters can wash away road foundations or close off sections that are inundated. In January, heavy rains led to major flash flooding along the Great Ocean Road, sweeping cars out to sea.

Value of road infrastructure at risk of damage in a 2030 low-emissions scenario. ( )

Bushfires can damage roads, destroy signs, lights and barriers and also compromise trees, leading to road closures.

These are largely concentrated around Melbourne but also include major corridors such as the Hume and Princes highways to the north and east.

Heat damage to rail network

Up to $10 billion worth of rail infrastructure, including tracks, stations, signals and depots, is at risk of damage, particularly from extreme heat as tracks expand and buckle. This can cause delays not only for commuters but for rail freight transport.

Value of rail infrastructure at risk of damage in a 2030 low-emissions scenario. ( )

The value of rail infrastructure at risk is the largest in Melbourne, Geelong and around regional corridors, particularly in the north-west.

Fire threatens energy supply

Power lines and power stations are at most risk of damage from bushfires and Infrastructure Victoria found $7 billion worth of energy assets at risk in 2030. These facilities are concentrated in the La Trobe Valley, Portland and in the north-west near Mildura.

Value of energy infrastructure at risk of damage in a 2030 low-emissions scenario. ( )

Climate risk is evolving

Climate change is already affecting Victoria. The state's annual average temperature has risen by 1.2 C since 1910. According to Victoria's Climate Science Report from 2024, warming has made heatwaves more intense, longer lasting and more frequent.

The state has become drier, while the intensity of short-duration extreme rainfall events is projected to increase. Fire weather and fire activity are also projected to increase in many regions of south-east Australia.



An estimated $5.3 billion in health assets, including hospitals, around the state will be at risk in 2030.

In January, as Victoria sweltered under heatwave conditions and bushfires burned throughout the state, a fast-moving grassfire in Natimuk stood out. For one, it moved so quickly that the aged care centre in town couldn't be evacuated in time.

New age of climate-driven fires The anatomy of a new kind of bushfire, fuelled by dangerous conditions in our changing climate.

Fortunately, firefighters were able to protect the site and its residents, but the nature of the fire highlights how existing systems were inadequate to meet a disaster of such magnitude.

Infrastructure Victoria modelled risk based on climate factors in 2030 and 2070 emissions scenarios. Across all natural disasters, risk exposure will increase as temperatures rise.

"The reality is we are experiencing extreme weather events now and that is only going to become more frequent in the future," Dr Spear said.

"Now is the time to start to take action to make sure our infrastructure is ready for that more frequent, extreme weather that we're going to have now and in the future."

The cost of action vs inaction

While the report paints a grim picture of the risks of a warming world, it also highlights the opportunities of acting before disaster hits.

"Funding high-priority, cost-effective infrastructure adaptation actions can save millions in recovery costs and lost productivity," Dr Spear said.

The Australian government spent an average of $1.6 billion each year on disaster recovery from 2012–13 to 2023–24, but the report found the return on pre-emptively acting is huge.

Climate-proofing infrastructure can seem like an overwhelming challenge, but even cleaning stormwater drains can offer a return of $5 in reduced damage for every dollar spent.

Jonathan Spear says acknowledging the growing risks and factoring them into infrastructure planning will allow the country to navigate the coming decades.

"We need to start taking action to make sure our infrastructure is going to continue to work in the face of the more extreme weather we're already facing.

"This is a challenge that we're going to have to work on over the coming decades as our climate becomes hotter and our weather becomes more extreme.

"We can factor this in when we're maintaining the infrastructure we already have and when we're building new infrastructure to make sure it's going to be suitable to work in these more frequent extreme weather conditions."

Note: Risk data by extreme weather event as shown in the header maps account for all infrastructure assets in that location rather than any singular network.

World.title: 'Two years to live': Why we used our super for weight loss surgery
World.content:
WARNING: This story contains pictures of a surgery.

At his heaviest, Fili Fili weighed about 300 kilograms.

He still doesn't know exactly how heavy he was — 300 was just the number his doctor gave him after he maxed out the scales at the clinic in 2017.

"You literally have two years left before you die," the doctor told him.

Those words haunted Fili and kick-started years of yo-yo dieting — losing and regaining weight — and exercise, often with his wife Natasha Narayan-Fili by his side.

"I actually got into dancing. I did salsa and zouk, I tried to get Tash into it, but we were both too fat to do it at the time. Our stomachs kept bumping and we couldn't hold each other," Fili said, as the couple laughed.

The Melbourne-based couple said they tried every weight loss fad under the sun, and under the guidance of their doctor, they finally decided to undergo weight loss surgery.

Fili Fili was told by his doctor his weight was a major health risk. (Supplied: Fili Fili)

In June 2025, Fili received a sleeve gastrectomy and Single Anastomosis Duodeno-ileal Bypass (SADI), an additional procedure that improves metabolism.

In a sleeve gastrectomy, commonly referred to as a gastric sleeve, a large portion of the stomach is removed.

Since maxing out the scales, Fili has lost 180kg.

In October 2025, Natasha underwent a sleeve gastrectomy and has since lost 30kg.

'It's given us opportunity'

Weight loss surgery has become an increasingly common option for people grappling with obesity, and gastric sleeves are the most popular procedure.

A surgeon makes small keyhole incisions in the abdomen and removes 70 to 80 per cent of the stomach.

The remaining stomach is reshaped into a narrow tube called a sleeve, which holds much less food, and patients feel full much faster.

In a sleeve gastrectomy a large part of the stomach is permanently removed. (ABC News: Cordelia Brown)

The surgery also reduces ghrelin production, a hunger hormone that helps suppress appetite.

Over time, the patient loses a significant amount of weight.

Fili and Natasha quickly noticed changes to their lives, including a huge reduction in living expenses.

"Our food bill was $600 every fortnight. Since surgery, I've never seen another grocery bill hit $200," Fili said.

"In summer, because I was such a massive person, I used to have the air con running 24-7 and that power bill was $500. But now our power bill is like $120 a month."

Since they've lost weight, they also feel more ready to consider having children.

"With the surgery it's given us opportunity to talk about it," Natasha said.

Gastric sleeve surgeries have become a common procedure for people dealing with obesity. (ABC News: Johnson Raela)

A Monash University and University of Sydney-led study published in the ANZ Journal of Surgery last year indicated bariatric surgeries, including sleeve gastrectomies, were generally safe.

Common risks of bariatric surgeries — an umbrella term for a range of surgical procedures used for weight loss — include gastric leaks, bleeding, infection, and long-term nutritional deficiencies.

If you or someone you know needs help: Butterfly National Helpline — 1800 33 4673 or visit www.butterfly.org.au

Eating Disorders Families Australia — 1300 195 626

Professionals Credentialed in Eating Disorders

Lifeline on 13 11 14

Suicide Call Back Service — 1300 659 467

Kids Helpline — 1800 55 1800

MensLine — 1300 78 99 78

Bariatric surgery is usually recommended if other weight loss options are not successful, according to Australian health advice website Healthdirect.

The Victorian government's Better Health Channel website says obesity surgery is "an effective, durable, evidence-based treatment for severe obesity and its associated health problems" but that it's "best considered as a tool".

"To obtain good long-term results, it is very important that patients are supported through their weight loss journey, to assist with permanent changes to their eating habits and lifestyle," it says.

Superannuation used for surgeries

The surgery can cost between $20,000 to $30,000 in Australia, and to afford it, more people are applying for and getting approved for a "compassionate release of superannuation" (CRS).

Fili and Natasha said they paid about $1,500 out of pocket for pre-operation appointments, but the majority of their surgery costs were covered by taking out the highest hospital cover in private medical insurance. Their remaining costs were covered by CRS.

"So [Fili's] was about $10,000 and my gap fee was $7,000," Natasha said.

Some patients are accessing their superannuation to fund gastric sleeve procedures. (ABC News: Johnson Raela)

According to the Australian Taxation Office, 13,930 people applied for CRS between 2024 and 2025. The ATO approved more than 13,200 applications and $254.9 million was paid out.

Wendy Brown, the clinical director of the Australia and New Zealand Bariatric Surgery Registry, said many people lacked private health insurance and needed options to cover the high costs of surgery.

"It is important that people do have the option to take out their super to have this life-changing surgery that allows people to live long enough to probably enjoy their super," Professor Brown said.

Wendy Brown is a bariatric surgeon and researches the optimal service delivery models for bariatric surgery. (ABC News)

Since 2018, the number of sleeve gastrectomy procedures in Australia has declined, and experts say the introduction of medications like Ozempic, Mounjaro and Wegovy has given people more options in their battle to lose weight.

But Professor Brown said that due to the cost-of-living crisis, people were looking at using CRS for cheaper surgery overseas.

"What can happen is once the money is released, the people can cancel their surgery, and they don't have to put it back into their super. They can then choose to use their super overseas. So I think there is a little loophole that maybe the ATO might need to look into," she said.

" That drives people to look for more cost-effective alternatives, and some of those alternatives are offshore, including places such as Türkiye. "

An ATO spokesperson said while there was no legal requirement for people to confirm they used their CRS release to pay for approved expenses, the agency was able to find out how the money was spent, including by requesting receipts, checking with providers or through tip-offs.

"If it is established that individuals have provided false or misleading information in their application, including in instances where they didn't intend to use the release on the approved expense, a range of consequences can apply for the individual," they said.

These included taxing the amount at their marginal tax rate rather than the concessional rate, changing their income tax position to reflect that the payment had been subject to illegal early access, or imposing penalties for making false or misleading statements.

Patients opt for overseas surgeries

Türkiye has emerged as a major hub for medical tourism, with more than 1.5 million people travelling there for procedures annually, and it's also a top five global destination for cosmetic surgery.

Social media accounts promote surgeries as a lavish travel experience — although Australian medical professionals warn that they carry risks.

With low wait times, surgeries cost 50-70 per cent less than in Australia and are packaged with tours of Istanbul's popular attractions, fine-dining experiences, luxury car transfers, and five-star hotel accommodation.

Watch the episode Weight loss surgery has become an increasingly common option for people grappling with obesity — and many are funding it using retirement savings.

Margaret Vaiouga had a sleeve gastrectomy in Türkiye in August 2025 and travelled with a medical tour group, at a cost of $11,500.

Ms Vaiouga says her experience matched social media portrayals of luxurious medical trips.

"The service, everything from the airport pick-up, is insane. We got picked up in these cool-as, fancy transits that took us to our hotel. It blew me away," she said.

"Compared to public hospitals, it was still flash and the rooms were just more spacious."

Margaret Vaiouga travelled overseas to have weight loss surgery. (Supplied: Margaret Vaiouga)

She decided to travel for the surgery after a car crash in early 2025 down to a sleeping disorder she'd developed from being overweight. She wasn't prepared to sit on a public waiting list for more than a year for the gastric sleeve.

Margaret weighed 130kg before surgery and is 88kg today.

"Before, when my husband would say, 'Hey, can you just watch the kids?' And I'd fall asleep. But now I'm doing more things with them, I take them out to the park."

Doctors warn of medical tourism risks

Although surgeries overseas are popular, doctors warn they come with risks.

They see people return from Türkiye with post-operative complications including leaks, infections and twisted stomachs.

Professor Brown, who works at Melbourne's Alfred Hospital, has seen the consequences of botched overseas surgeries.

"We've certainly had people that have landed on our doorstep very unwell, having been put on a plane back from Türkiye and from other overseas countries for that matter, really almost too unwell to travel," she said.

"We've had to care for them. And of course we do, but it's not ideal for the patient, and it's not ideal for our healthcare system either".

Melbourne-based bariatric surgeon Dan Foley said overseas hospitals could be making cost savings through cheaper medical equipment.

"They are either using a different product, which is much cheaper, or the company that makes this product and sells it to them is selling it to them for a significant discount. I'm not sure which one of those two it is," Dr Foley said.

"I would presume that in other countries where they're doing the surgery significantly cheaper, that everybody is on a significantly lower wage, or they're utilising people who don't have quite the same level of qualification and experience."

Dan Foley is a bariatric surgeon who performs sleeve gastrectromies. (ABC News: Hugo Hodge)

Professor Brown urged people considering surgery to consider the support they'd receive afterwards.

"Do it in a way that's really going to support you to get the best outcome you can," she said.

"And that usually involves working with a surgeon who recognises that you need a team around you and that you need ongoing care and you need to be supported throughout your life to make sure that you get that best result you can."

She also said patients needed to work with their doctors to adjust their nutrition and manage any problems following surgery.

Teens resort to obesity surgery Jake Butcher was 16 years old and weighed 172 kilograms when he was warned he may not live to his 20s. Now he's one of a growing number of teens turning their lives around with surgery.

"Because you can't eat as much and because we're changing your stomach, you can't absorb things like iron and B12 and vitamin D and calcium in particular as much as you used to," Professor Brown said.

"Down the track things can also go wrong, the sleeve can stretch, the sleeve can twist, you can start getting heartburn and reflux.

"Having a connection back into your surgical team makes managing those little hiccups over time much easier than if your surgical team is well overseas and they haven't made any arrangements to look after you once you get home."

For Fili and Natasha, medical tourism was never an option.

"We never talked about it. We saw all the other people, we saw social media, but it never crossed our mind," Fili said.

His advice to people considering surgery overseas was to make an informed decision after research.

"There are great aftercare plans here [in Australia] that you might not necessarily get overseas."

World.title: Young investors accept 'party had to end' but rethink plans after CGT changes
World.content:
Vanessa has a plan to get ahead financially: work hard, save carefully and invest early.

The 28-year-old high school teacher started buying exchange-traded funds (ETFs) at 18, hoping it would help her build financial security, when the housing market felt increasingly out of reach.

Originally from Melbourne, she moved to Margaret River in Western Australia, where she and her partner now live in a campervan on a vacant block of land they bought last year, while they save to build a house.

Alongside full-time teaching, she teaches in a university program, tutors and runs an online store.

"I wouldn't volunteer to do this much work," she said.

" I'm just trying to build a home, and be safe, and have somewhere to live. "

Vanessa has about $120,000 invested across global and local ETFs, but the federal government's proposed capital gains tax (CGT) changes have forced her to rethink her financially planning.

Loading...

"I do think it's a step in the right direction," she said of the budget's tax reforms.

The federal government said the budget measures are designed to make the tax system fairer, improve housing affordability and help younger Australians into the property market.

Under the proposed changes, the 50 per cent capital gains tax discount would be replaced with cost-base indexation from July 1, 2027 for assets held for more than 12 months, with earlier gains remaining under the current rules.

Instead of effectively halving a taxable capital gain, the purchase price would be adjusted for inflation and tax would apply to the remaining "real" gain. The government also plans a 30 per cent minimum tax on real capital gains.

For investors who are already in the market — such as Vanessa — any capital gains made until July next year will be eligible for the 50 per cent CGT discount, while gains made after that date will be subject to the new scheme.

CGT discount benefits skew old and rich: PBO, Treasury

Vanessa said she is worried about the impact of the CGT changes on people who are investing in shares because property is already too expensive.

"For growth assets like ETFs, shares or crypto, the gain can sometimes be much bigger than inflation," she said.

"So inflation indexation does not reduce the taxable gain as much as the old 50 per cent discount did."

The impact will vary. Indexation may be better when inflation is high and returns are low, while the current discount may be more generous for high-growth assets such as shares, ETFs and crypto.

Official analysis suggests younger investors are not the main beneficiaries of the existing CGT discount.

Loading

The Parliamentary Budget Office estimates the discount will cost the budget $21.8 billion in 2025–26, with about 82 per cent of the benefit flowing to the top 10 per cent of income earners and almost 60 per cent to the top 1 per cent.

Treasury analysis also shows the benefit skews older, with those aged 50 to 69 receiving the greatest share by age.

That does not mean younger ETF investors are unaffected, but it suggests they are not the main beneficiaries of the current system.

Narrowing the tax gap between wages and investment income

Helen Hodgson, an adjunct professor of tax at Curtin University, said the reforms were one part of making the system fairer by narrowing the gap between how income from work and income from investments are taxed.

Can Labor's tax changes fix housing mess? The Albanese government and the opposition both want to turn back the clock on the Australian tax system.

She said the existing capital gains tax discount had disproportionately benefited older and wealthier Australians, who were more likely to have the spare cash to invest in assets such as rental properties.

But she said tax reform alone would not resolve the wider pressures on young Australians, including housing costs and student debt.

Professor Helen Hodgson says the reforms are one part of making the system fairer. (ABC News: Aran Hart)

Matt Nolan, a senior research manager at e61, said the reforms should not be seen as a complete answer to intergenerational inequality.

"When I look at these tax changes, they don't really seem to have too much to do with intergenerational fairness itself," he said.

He said the changes were more about whether income from investments should be taxed more like income from work.

"What they are trying to tackle is the idea of someone who earns a wage and invests in their human capital paying the same tax as someone who invests in stocks and earns their income in that way."

Mr Nolan said the broader intergenerational problem was about weak income growth, rising spending pressures and whether the economy could generate stronger opportunities for younger Australians.

First home buyers at auctions after tax changes The government says changes to negative gearing and the capital gains tax discount are aimed at levelling the playing field for young buyers bidding against property investors.

"The tax questions are important, and they're important for fairness, but not so much for intergenerational equity," he said.

For Vanessa, that distinction matters, but it does not remove the sting.

She has accepted the government's argument that investor tax breaks helped distort the housing market, and said some reform was probably inevitable.

"I know why it's happening now," she said.

" I think for our society overall, the party had to end eventually. Kind of sucks we're at that edge of the end of the party, but it had to end. "

'Makes you second-guess what you've done'

For Daniel Woodcock, a 36-year-old structural engineer from Western Australia, investing in ETFs was not about getting rich quickly.

After a marriage separation and a period of paying down debt, he saw them as a way to build financial security without taking on the large debts often required to buy property.

With ETFs, he said, he has been investing gradually, hoping the gains would compound over time and later allow him to sell down modest amounts if he wanted to reduce work in later years, before accessing superannuation.

Daniel Woodcock had a plan to sell off his ETF investments to help fund his retirement. (ABC News: Aran Hart)

"It was more financial security," he said.

But Daniel said the proposed 30 per cent minimum tax on real capital gains accruing from July 1, 2027, had changed the equation.

"With the new system, any capital gain after July next year, it's 30 per cent [minimum tax rate], which is quite a big difference, especially if you're only pulling out a small amount to live in the future," he said.

He said the changes could mean investing more now, working longer, accepting less later, or rethinking his strategy altogether.

" It just makes you second-guess what you've done … with investment, time is a huge contribution factor. "

The government's own budget papers show the 30 per cent minimum tax is designed to reduce the benefit of investors deferring capital gains until years when their marginal tax rates are lower.

Experts say older Australians have been more likely to have the spare cash to buy rental properties. (ABC News: Ian Cutmore)

Mr Nolan from e61 said Daniel's concern was fair but his bigger concern was the way long-term capital gains are taxed all at once, even if they build up over many years.

"That's income that's been earned over 20 years, but it's been taxed like it all happens at once," he said.

"It's lumpy."

Mr Nolan said the government should consider income averaging, so tax better reflects the period over which the gain was earned.

Income averaging means spreading a capital gain across the years it was built up, rather than taxing it all in the single year the asset is sold.

"I don't think the minimum tax rate is the right approach," he said.

Rentvestors say they are not property speculators

Darcy Mangan rents in Sydney and owns one newly built investment property in Brisbane.

The 34-year-old said "rentvesting" was the only way he could get his foot into the housing market.

Darcy Mangan "rentvests", owning an investment property in Brisbane while renting in Sydney. (Supplied)

Rentvesting is a strategy where people rent where they want or need to live, while buying a property in a more affordable area.

"I couldn't afford to live close to where I work," he said.

" I couldn't afford a loan without rental income. The only path that was open to me was investment. "

Because Darcy bought before federal budget night on May 12, his existing negative gearing arrangements are set to be grandfathered.

Loading

But his concern is what happens if he eventually sells the Brisbane property to buy a home to live in.

Under the proposed changes, any capital gains Darcy makes up to July 1, 2027 would still be taxed under the current CGT rules, including the 50 per cent discount for assets held longer than 12 months.

But gains made after that date would fall under the new system, where the 50 per cent discount would be replaced with cost-base indexation.

The treasurer has said rentvesting will still be available for new builds. (ABC News: John Gunn)

"If I do sell later on, the taxation that's going to come out of that capital gain, depending on how much house prices go up, could be much more than what it was with the 50 per cent discount," he said.

"That's going to mean that I'm likely to have less capability to get a principal place of residence."

Only small portion of under-35s rentvesting, says treasurer

Treasurer Jim Chalmers has rejected criticism that the changes unfairly punish young investors, arguing the reforms remove "one of the big distortions" from the market and create "a fairer, more neutral treatment of investment".

Economists divided on property prices Some economists are forecasting price falls of up to 5 per cent as a result of measures to reduce intergenerational housing inequality.

He said rentvesting would still be available for new builds and noted rentvestors represented a small proportion of people under 35.

The government says the reforms will help around 75,000 Australians into home ownership over the next decade, while Treasury modelling suggests house prices will grow by around 2 per cent less over a couple of years than they otherwise would have.

For Darcy, rentvesting was not about building a property portfolio, it was a response to housing unaffordability.

"My biggest frustration with the changes is that there's no nuance," he said.

World.title: Should the tax system reward those who can afford to take risks?
World.content:
Visiting a play centre with my kids over the weekend, I overheard two couples talking about the tax changes in the budget.

They were clearly both small business owners who were worried about what it would mean for them, especially the capital gains tax (CGT) changes if they sold up in the future.

One person seemed very well informed about business tax rules, but even he got a number of key facts about the proposed tax changes completely wrong.

Having spent six hours focused on those tax changes in the budget lock-up, along with many hours reading analyst notes since, I was tempted to thrust myself into their discussion, but it wasn't the time or the place.

This is.

The first thing to say is that the legislation for these changes hasn't even reached parliament, let alone gone through committee processes, debate, amendments and passage into law.

In response to a pre-budget backlash from parts of the tech start-up community, the government announced on budget night that it would consider special arrangements or carve-outs for new businesses.

Treasurer Jim Chalmers says the changes will "rebalance" the tax system to help workers. (ABC News: Matt Roberts)

So we don't actually know exactly what the final arrangements will be.

The second thing is that the interaction of tax rules around capital gains, trusts, instant asset write-offs and loss carry back is complicated — if it wasn't, tens of thousands of accountants would be out of work.

Bearing in mind that no-one fully understands all the detail, which is likely to change before these changes become law, let's focus instead on the core principle.

High income earners should pay at least 30 per cent tax

If you had to distil the tax changes around negative gearing, capital gains and trusts down to one overarching principle, it's that higher income earners should pay at least 30 cents in the dollar in tax on their profits/earnings.

As Treasurer Jim Chalmers said on budget night, "This will help rebalance a system which is more generous to assets than it is to labour."

Unsurprisingly, howls of protest have been quick to emerge from those who do earn the bulk of their income from owning assets rather than working.

Loading

For all the breathless commentary and social memes about 47 per cent tax rates, the reality is that no-one will pay that on their nominal capital gains.

For a start, the 47 per cent tax claim confuses marginal tax rates — what you pay on each extra dollar earned — with average tax rates, which look at what percentage of their income someone actually pays in tax.

Beyond that, indexation means that investors get a discount for inflation and will only be taxed on their so-called "real gains".

Loading

That's something wage and salary earners don't get, even when their pay fails to keep up with rising prices, as has been the case for much of the past decade or so.

This overarching principle of evening up the score between wage earners and asset owners is why government has also brought in a 30 per cent minimum tax rate for discretionary trust income and the same floor rate for real capital gains (that is the profit after the indexation discount for inflation).

Why should a nurse pay the same tax rate as her employer?

Let's take a look at how this overarching principle might apply in practice.

Say you've got Jane, who works as a nurse in a dental practice, and John who owns the practice through a discretionary trust.

Let's say she earns $100,000 a year and doesn't have any deductions. That means she pays 30 cents in the dollar of tax on the bulk of her income, 16 cents on another part and no tax on the first $18,200 she earns.

On average, including the 2 per cent Medicare levy, Jane pays just under 23 per cent tax across her earnings.

After expenses, John's practice clears a $400,000 annual profit.

If he personally took all those earnings as dividends, he'd pay 45 cents in the dollar on everything over $190,000, 37 cents in the dollar on earnings between $135,001 to $190,000, 30 cents in the dollar on $45,001-$90,000, 16 cents in the dollar on earnings between $18,201-$45,000, and nothing on earnings under the tax-free threshold.

John would pay an average tax rate of just under 39 per cent, including the 2 per cent Medicare levy across all his income.

But if his discretionary trust spreads the distributions, John and his family end up paying much less tax.

Let's say his wife doesn't work and he has two adult children studying at university.

Finally, a tax fight that actually means something Labor and the Liberals are offering imperfect but undeniably bold alternative visions for the tax system. It's nice to have something to talk about.

If John's trust paid him $175,000, then the highest tax rate he pays is 37 per cent and his average tax rate goes from 39 to 28 per cent.

Let's say his wife gets $135,000. On that she pays an average tax rate of just over 25 per cent, not much above Jane.

Each of John's two adult kids get $45,000 to live on while they're at university. The first $18,200 of that is tax free for both of them, while the rest is taxed at 16 cents in the dollar.

They pay an average tax rate of just under 12 per cent, including the 2 per cent Medicare levy.

Overall, John's family is paying a tax rate on their combined $400,000 income of just over 23 per cent — more or less the same as Jane, who earns a quarter as much.

John probably has to pay accountants and lawyers several thousand dollars a year to maintain the trust but, as you can see, it more than pays for itself in tax savings.

Loading

However, if the government's minimum trust tax laws pass, then John, his wife and the two adult kids will effectively pay 30 per cent on everything they receive from the trust, plus the Medicare levy.

Their family tax bill will go up from just under $94,000 to $128,000 — $34,000 a year isn't exactly loose change, so you can see why the people who use these structures are dead against the changes.

But what about reward for risk-taking?

Many might argue that the dental practice owner deserves to keep more of their income. After all, they've probably invested hundreds of thousands, perhaps even millions, of dollars in equipment, property, advertising, staff training, not to mention the other recurrent costs of running the business.

If something goes wrong, they're the one on the hook — well, with a trust or corporate structure, often it's their creditors (the people they owe money too) financially on the hook.

But that overlooks a couple of things.

Critics of the budget have said investors prepared to take risks should be rewarded. (Unsplash: Dylan Gillis)

Jane's contribution to the enterprise isn't without risk either.

She could be fired and struggle to find a new job. Or she could get injured or ill and never be able to sell her labour again.

Also, it may be that Jane would love to take the risk of opening her own dental practice. Maybe she'd do an even better job than John, but where is she going to get the capital to get it started?

The Assistant Minister for Productivity, Competition, Charities and Treasury, Andrew Leigh, who is a former economics professor, gave a recent speech about how inequality can inhibit productivity.

'Inefficiency with a human face' Is reducing inequality and increasing social mobility one of Australia's best paths to improving our lacklustre economic productivity performance?

In it, he cited academic research that demonstrates what most of us intuitively know.

"Bell et al (2019) show that children born to parents in the top 1 per cent of the income distribution are 10 times as likely to become inventors as those born to families with below-median incomes," Leigh notes.

"Those gaps persist even among children with similar mathematics performance in early life."

In other words, kids who grow up with money benefit from a familial safety net that allows them to take risks in their lives, like being an inventor.

No doubt the same applies to being an investor or business founder.

Housing tax reform is one part of bigger project to fix Australia At the turn of the century, "aspiration" described Australians who wanted to put their kids into private school and university, and to build their wealth by getting an investment property or two. Today, it means something humbler; millions of younger Australians simply aspire to own a home one day, to have some shelter.

If you have wealthier parents, chances are you have easier access to capital — you don't have to beg to borrow from a bank or wow an angel investor.

That's not to say there aren't rags to riches stories, but they're less common than folklore would have you believe.

So, yes, society should reward people who take risks to start new enterprises, but we also shouldn't forget the relative privilege that allowed many of those people to take those risks.

The same principle applies to investing.

While some small-time investors might strike it lucky, without the capital to start with, the financial expertise and, dare I say it, the connections and inside knowledge, the chances of your average day trader consistently beating the big investment houses are vanishingly small.

Small but influential group affected

It's no surprise then that Treasury figures show around 90 per cent of private trust wealth is held by the wealthiest 10 per cent of households (those with a net worth around $2.3 million and above), while around a third of capital gains went to people in the top 1 per cent of income earners over their working lives with more than half going to the top 10 per cent.

With relatively few Australians greatly affected, the noise around the proposals has been deafening over the past week.

But when you consider the relative power and influence of those who are, it's not surprising.

Does budget change on trusts go too far? The federal budget includes a new 30 per cent minimum tax on discretionary trusts. Experts say it is not just the ultra-wealthy that will be hit.

John is far more likely to be out there campaigning to keep his $34,000 tax break than Jane is to get a modest tax offset funded by removing it.

The problem with complex tax changes is that the fundamental issues can easily be lost beneath a forest of detail, misinformation and half-truths.

It's a challenge that buried Bill Shorten and Chris Bowen in the 2019 election.

With early polling showing the initial reaction to the budget is deeply negative, Anthony Albanese and Jim Chalmers will be hoping it's not a case of history repeating.

World.title: 'I wish I were dead': The heartbreaking toll of Australia's favourite pastime
World.content:
Australians are the world's biggest gamblers per capita, with $1,500 lost per adult each year.

In a nation that boasts gambling as a national pastime, around three in five Australians bet at least once a year, and one in five engage in risky gambling.

But beyond the statistics are deeply personal stories of addiction, loss and lasting harm.

Warning: This story contains discussion of addiction and suicide.

We spoke to three people about the moment they realised gambling had changed their lives.

The moment I realised I had an addiction

Carolyn's story

I only realised I had an addiction when I went to prison.

To me, addiction meant drugs and alcohol, not gambling. I just thought I was a silly old woman who couldn't stop.

I'd had two marriages fall apart, and I swore I'd never fall in love again — then I started a new job and fell in love with the boss.

He was two years older than me and a real charmer. I knew in my heart that he'd never fall for me, but I really liked him. Every time he didn't have somewhere to go at night, he'd ask me to join him, and we'd inevitably end up at the pokies.

The more I went out with him, the more I got addicted. The more I lost, the more I kept going back, and so I stole money from the company to chase my losses.

Carolyn would spend hours using poker machines. (ABC: Anna Levy)

It got to the point where I didn't care whether I won or lost; I just had to be there. I had to be in front of those machines.

They're just mind-numbing; they take away all your stresses. At the time, my father was very ill, and the machines took that pain away. All the worries about my life, my work — everything, really — would go away as well.

If you or anyone you know needs help, contact: National Gambling Helpline on 1800 858 858

Lifeline on 13 11 14

Headspace on 1800 650 890

Many a night I drove out of the club and thought, I could just take my life here and stop all this. If it weren't for my children, I wouldn't be here now. I just couldn't do that to my children.

I stole $400,000 over seven years. Eventually, my boss' daughter-in-law started working with the company and she picked it up. I got sacked, which was fair enough.

They charged me the day that my father was in the hospital, dying. The police rang me and said, "We need to speak to you". They were very kind.

They charged me, photographed me, and fingerprinted me. I met the barrister for two hours at Legal Aid, and everything I told her about gambling, she didn't believe. She kept asking, "Are you sure you didn't spend the money on luxuries?"

As I was sentenced, my children were crying. That's the part that hurts the most, to think that I'd let them down.

I was 64 years old. I'd never had a parking ticket in my life. And here I was in the bowels of a courtroom, waiting to go to prison.

Even though it was horrendous and I dearly wish it had never happened, my experience in prison saved my life. I had a counsellor who helped me a lot.

When he explained what addiction was, the weight that lifted off my shoulders was enormous. I started crying. I was actually hysterical to think that they did this to me, these machines did this to me, this wasn't me.

It just blew my mind, and then I started getting angry, and I thought, right, let's do something about this, let's try to help other people not end up where I did.

"If it hadn't been for prison and the counsellor, I'd probably still be gambling," Carolyn says. (ABC: Anna Levy)

Now, I'm a lived-experience performer, along with another lady whose husband was a gambler. She and I do a two-person performance where we tell our story.

I've paid back all the money I stole, so I owe the company nothing. But I've got nothing. Without gambling, I would have had my own little unit, but I've got nothing and that breaks my heart.

I take full responsibility for what I did, but nobody told me about the dangers of these machines. Nobody told me that they actually set them up to make sure you become addicted.

I wear the blame, of course I do. But I won't wear it all. I refuse to wear it all.

I think people need to hear from us, the people who have been harmed, to understand that this is an addiction. If you're in it, you can survive it. You can get help.

Every day it's a battle. But the battle's got to be won.

The moment my dad left me behind

Sarah's story*

My dad worked in finance his whole life, so he was very familiar with numbers and odds. That's why I was always so surprised about how far he went with the pokies, that this intelligent man could be so captivated by these machines.

He would have two machines going at the same time, and he'd be feeding $50 notes into them. He'd sit there and say to me, "This machine's about to pay off". He thought he could read the algorithm, though he clearly couldn't.

He'd easily spend $500 in a day, if not more. His total losses would be in the tens if not hundreds of thousands.

Going for broke Shaun Micallef examines Australia's complex relationship with gambling, discovering how we became the world's biggest losers and what this rapid expansion means for our future. Stream now on iview.

I have this very distinct memory of us going on a family holiday to Adelaide. I was about 14 and completely obsessed with cricket.

Dad and I went to Adelaide Oval to watch a cricket match on the first day of the test, and I was so excited to go. It was probably the only father-daughter day out in my life.

We had a fantastic day together and it was really special. Then, as we headed back into the city, Dad said, "I just want to pop into the casino". He told me to sit in the casino lobby and that he wouldn't be long.

Half an hour passed, then another. I couldn't go in to find him because I was under 18. He was in there for about two hours altogether.

I just sat, waiting for him, thinking, how can you do that to your kid?

That day should have been one of the happiest memories of my life with my dad. But it was completely tainted.

It's so hurtful to see someone you care about, someone who should know better, being completely and utterly entranced by a dangerous product.

"When someone has an addiction, they don't feel like they're yours anymore," Sarah says. (ABC: Anna Levy)

COVID-19 was a bit of a circuit-breaker for my dad; there was no way to get that pokies dopamine hit during lockdown.

Since then, I've worked on my mum to try to stop him from going back, because he won't listen to me. He still gambles in other ways, like Keno and horses. I don't know for certain that he's stopped with the pokies.

I don't know what we're going to find when he dies, in terms of the finances. The house has been paid off for forever and it's a strong asset, but there's every chance in the world that he's used it as leverage.

There's only so much fighting you can do, because as far as my dad is concerned, there's nothing wrong with gambling.

I wish people realised how insidious the industry is, how it targets people and their vulnerabilities.

My dad's brain was rewired by poker machines, and that's exactly what they are designed to do.

It just makes me so, so sad.

The moment I fell out of orbit

Angus' story*

I was in my late 40s when it all started to unravel.

I was dealing with a lot of trauma and stress from a number of issues that happened in a very short period of time. My best friend died, my dog died, I was under significant work pressure, and I found out one of my children was having substance abuse issues.

My vice was online gambling on racing, which is available 24/7.

I went from using my own money to borrowing money, to getting credit from financial institutions, and then eventually breaking the law to obtain money. It was a pretty horrible escalation.

I believe every person's got an orbit, and in that orbit is who you are as a person: your character, your values, your family and your friends.

In my case, as soon as I borrowed money and lied about it, I stepped out of my orbit. And I kept stepping out further and further until I couldn't get back.

"I was encouraged and incentivised to keep gambling by both the banks and the gambling companies," Angus says. (ABC: Anna Levy)

My addiction was hidden from every single soul in my network. Nobody knew. It was just too embarrassing, too shameful to discuss, even with my best mates. You feel like you're the only one, that you're a disgrace.

I was living in complete isolation, not being able to sleep, and using alcohol as a way to ease the pain. I would wake up every day and say to myself, "I wish I were dead. Why didn't I die in my sleep?"

It was a complete loss of hope, a hole so deep that you are unable to see the light.

Fate intervened at a critical moment and I was taken to hospital. I ended up in a facility where they spoke about addiction and how the brain functions, and it was like an awakening for me.

I realised, hang on, I'm not evil. I am a good guy, I'm just sick.

That was the thing that ultimately saved me. I haven't consumed alcohol or gambled ever since.

Then the legal stuff started coming at me. I spent time in prison, which was a terrible experience.

When I got out, I started to really sink my teeth into advocacy work. Seeing what happened in my circumstances, I didn't want any other person to have to go through it.

I accept responsibility for my actions, and I have to live with the consequences. But the one burning question I have when I look back is: how was this allowed to happen?

Government accused of 'burying' response to landmark gambling report A long-awaited response to an inquiry that called for a gambling advertising ban has been tabled on budget day, prompting accusations the government is trying to bury the document.

The government, the banks, and the gambling companies are failing us. Even though they possess the technology and systems to identify gambling harm, they don't do anything about it.

I nearly took my own life over gambling because we just don't have the safeguards in place to protect vulnerable people.

I'm on the cusp of finding my orbit again. I look at how far I've come and I'm pretty proud of that.

But self-forgiveness is really hard when it's had such an impact on the people I love and care for. They didn't ask for this, and I didn't want to give them this.

I just lost my way. As many people do.

* Some names have been altered to preserve anonymity.
